mappings.note: Krishna as the Pandavas' helper - a personality within the Mahabharata, which is LO-161's subject.
Ravana as Sita's abductor; an event inside the Ramayana, so LO-161.
Hanuman aiding Rama and Lakshmana - again a character and episode from the epic.
Names a tribal community holding its own epic version: the community is the answer (LO-166) and the epics the material (LO-161).

The Pancha Pandavar shrine kept by Irula tribals in the Nilgiris - a named community's appropriation of the epic (LO-166, LO-161). Not LO-160, which is for historical sites used as evidence of the past.
K. S. Singh as director of the People of India project; a fact about the survey of India's communities, so LO-166.
India holding about 18 per cent of the world's people - the scale that makes the diversity intelligible, hence LO-166.
Names a spice used countrywide; the shared element beneath varied regional food.
Cotton as the other main sari fabric besides silk - part of the dress-variety strand of LO-166.
Aurobindo's principle that unity in diversity has been normal to India; the chapter's thesis quoted, so LO-166.
Lists what strikes visitors - landscapes, dress, food, languages, customs. A direct description of India's human diversity.
What the People of India project was: a survey of 4,635 communities and their languages and scripts; the documentation of diversity, so LO-166.
Food as the worked example of unity in diversity - thousands of dishes on a shared base of grains and spices.
Why rice, wheat and millets count as staples; the common food foundation across regions, hence LO-166.
The sari as one garment shown in countless weaves and drapes - the dress example of the chapter's thesis.
Three non-dress uses of a sari from the illustrations; everyday ingenuity within the shared tradition, so LO-166.
Festivals as the third worked example - one occasion, many regional names and customs.
The Panchatantra's place in Indian AND world literature: an ancient Indian work (LO-161) whose travel abroad is contact with other regions (LO-173).
The epics' central theme of heroes restoring dharma: the works' content (LO-161) and the value they turn on (LO-175).
How the epics moved beyond Sanskrit into regional languages and oral traditions: the works (LO-161) recast across a diverse country (LO-166).
The place of the epics in tribal cultural life, tying epic heroes to local history - communities first (LO-166), then the epics (LO-161).
K. S. Singh's point that folklore has the Pandavas visiting almost every part of India: shared narrative binding diverse regions (LO-166) through the epic (LO-161).
'Diversity does not divide, it enriches' applied to Indian culture - the healthy-attitude clause of LO-166.
Why a country of 1.4 billion over varied terrain should be diverse; an explanation of the diversity LO-166 asks pupils to describe.
How weaves and printed designs multiply sari styles - the mechanism behind the dress diversity, so LO-166.
Summarises the Ramayana's plot - the contents of a named epic, hence LO-161 rather than the diversity outcome.
The Pandava-Kaurava struggle for Hastinapur; the Mahabharata's central conflict, so LO-161.
How the epics' sub-plots weigh duty and consequence: the works' construction (LO-161) and the ethical ideas they explore (LO-175).
How shared ingredients yield endless dishes - the food case stated as a general mechanism, so LO-166.
Why England and France banned chintz: an Indian craft (LO-174) so successful abroad that foreign states acted against it (LO-173).
Literature as another face of unity in diversity - many languages (LO-166) sharing epic characters and moral concerns (LO-161).
Folk versions as evidence of active adaptation by many communities: cultural interaction (LO-166) worked on the epics (LO-161).
Elaborates unity in diversity through food and clothing together; the chapter's thesis at long-answer length, so LO-166.
Makara Sankranti's many names over one harvest theme as 'Many in the One' - the festival case, again LO-166.
How the epics knit diverse regions together: the works and their adaptations (LO-161) creating a shared framework across communities (LO-166).
The Panchatantra as one becoming many and what that says about cultural transmission - an Indian work (LO-161) crossing linguistic and national borders (LO-173).
The sari's adaptability read for both practicality and identity; the dress strand of the diversity argument.
'Diversity enriches' as the chapter's organising idea, argued across languages, food, dress, festivals and literature - LO-166.
The project's figures on languages, scripts, communities and migration as the evidence for India's diversity; LO-166, since the item is about what those numbers show.
How a shared base of grains and spices supports distinct regional cuisines - the food case argued in full, so LO-166.
The epics' constant questioning of right and wrong as the source of their lasting appeal: their content (LO-161) and the dharma they examine (LO-175).
Choosing two examples to explain unity in diversity to an outsider - the pupil must select and justify from the chapter's diversity material, hence LO-166.
Tribal versions unsettling the great-versus-little tradition split: mutual influence between communities (LO-166) carried by the epics (LO-161).
Asks what the underlying unity actually consists of - shared values, staples, festival themes and stories. A synthesis of the chapter's diversity argument, so LO-166.
Food-festival case with biryani, dhokla, macher jhol and idli on a shared rice-and-spice base; the item names unity in diversity in its answer, so LO-166.
Students from four states finding their harvest festivals differ in name but not in purpose - the festival case as a classroom scenario, again LO-166.
A designer contrasting Banarasi and Kanjivaram weaves that are both plainly saris; the dress case as a scenario, so LO-166.
Hundreds of languages set against link languages and translated epics: linguistic diversity (LO-166) bridged by shared texts (LO-161).
